stories.headline: NASDAQ SLIDES INTO CORRECTION AS NVIDIA FALLS FOR A THIRD STRAIGHT SESSION, S&P 500 DROPS 1.9%
stories.body: The S&P 500 closed down 1.91% at 7,417 and the Nasdaq 100 fell 2.65% to 27,197, with the Nasdaq Composite now more than 10% below its October 6 record and officially in correction territory; Nvidia dropped roughly 4.1% for its third consecutive decline since Jensen Huang's resignation, dragging the broader tech complex lower.
stories.explain: A 10% drawdown from a closing high is the textbook definition of a correction, and the index got there almost entirely on the back of a handful of AI-linked mega-caps repricing at once rather than a broad economic deterioration. Because Nvidia alone carries an outsized weight in both the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100, its leadership-crisis selloff mechanically pulls both cap-weighted benchmarks down even for investors who hold none of the stock directly, which is why the decline looks much more severe on the index tape than in the median S&P 500 constituent.

stories.headline: ANTHROPIC'S IPO VALUATION REPORTEDLY NEEDS TO COME DOWN FROM $1.5 TRILLION TARGET AS AI SKEPTICISM SPREADS
stories.body: Three major investors planning to participate in Anthropic's IPO told the Wall Street Journal the company's valuation will likely need to fall below the roughly $1.5 trillion level analysts had forecast, with one strategist saying a lower price is now effectively required to clear the deal; some reports suggest the offering could be postponed altogether.
stories.explain: An IPO's valuation isn't set by the company alone — it's negotiated through bookbuilding, where anchor investors signal the price and size they'll actually commit capital at, and when enough of them balk at a number, the lead underwriters have to mark it down to get the deal done rather than risk it falling flat on the first trading day. Anthropic testing a lower price right as Nvidia's AI-capex narrative is under its own pressure shows the markdown isn't company-specific — it's the broader AI investment complex repricing the multiple the market will pay for projected, not realized, cash flows.

stories.headline: HOUSE COMMITTEE CHAIRS' CLOSED-DOOR BRIEFING REQUEST WITH JENSEN HUANG SET FOR NOV. 18 KEEPS ESPIONAGE QUESTIONS LIVE
stories.body: Three House committee chairs who requested a closed-door briefing with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang over his contacts with a Megaspeed executive U.S. intelligence agencies reportedly flagged as a Chinese intelligence asset are still awaiting word on his attendance, with the session requested for Wednesday, Nov. 18; neither Huang nor Nvidia has been charged, and both have denied wrongdoing.
stories.explain: Congressional scrutiny over export-control compliance and foreign-influence risk doesn't need an indictment to move a stock — the mere prospect of new disclosure obligations, trade-secret exposure, or future chip-export restrictions widens the range of outcomes investors have to price, which shows up as a higher equity risk premium and lower multiple even before any finding of fact. That overhang, layered on top of Huang's resignation, is why Nvidia's selloff has outpaced the broader AI-stock decline rather than tracking it one-for-one.

stories.headline: DECEMBER HIKE ODDS NEAR 85% ON CME FEDWATCH AS WARSH'S FED LEAVES RATES UNCHANGED BUT STOPS SHORT OF RULING ONE OUT
stories.body: CME Group's FedWatch tool continues to show roughly an 85% probability of a quarter-point hike at the Dec. 8-9 FOMC meeting after the Fed under Chair Kevin Warsh held rates at 3.75%-4% in October on a 10-2 vote, with governors Cook and Hammack dissenting in favor of a hike; Warsh declined to commit to December tightening but left the door open.
stories.explain: FedWatch backs out these odds from 30-Day Fed Funds futures prices, which trade at 100 minus the market's expected average fed funds rate for the contract month — so the 85% figure is a real-time, tradable bet on the outcome, not a survey of what economists think Warsh will do. A 10-2 dissent in favor of hiking, rather than toward holding or cutting, tells you the hawkish wing of the committee is already outvoted but gaining ground, which is exactly the setup that keeps futures pricing a hike as the base case even without an explicit commitment from the chair.

stories.headline: WTI SLIDES 3.7% TO $85 ON EASING IRAN TENSIONS; GOLD SLIPS, DOLLAR FIRMS ON HAWKISH FED REPRICING
stories.body: WTI crude fell 3.71% to $85 a barrel as renewed diplomatic signals around Iran eased supply-risk premiums built into the price, while gold slipped 0.29% to $3,859 an ounce and the dollar index (DXY) firmed 0.14% to 103.58 as the roughly 85% odds of a December Fed hike kept real yields supported.
stories.explain: Oil's move today is a supply-side story — easing geopolitical risk lowers the probability-weighted disruption premium traders had built into the price, independent of anything happening in equities or rates. Gold's small decline is the more familiar mechanism: a firmer dollar raises the effective price for non-dollar buyers and higher-for-longer rate expectations raise the opportunity cost of holding a zero-coupon asset, so both pressured gold in the same direction even as equities sold off for an unrelated reason.

watchlist: Jensen Huang's closed-door briefing with House committee chairs, requested for Nov. 18 — first real signal on whether he appears and what it reveals about the espionage allegations
Anthropic's IPO terms — reported pressure from anchor investors to price well below the $1.5 trillion target, with some reports suggesting a possible postponement
Fed's Dec. 8-9 FOMC meeting — hike odds near 85% on CME FedWatch under Chair Kevin Warsh after an October 10-2 vote with two dissents favoring a hike
Nasdaq Composite's correction — now more than 10% below its Oct. 6 record high, with Nvidia's continued slide the single biggest swing factor
November retail sales and jobs data — the next hard data the Fed weighs before the December decision

deepDive.title: Why Anthropic's IPO Is Reportedly Getting Marked Down Before It Even Prices
content: Today's brief includes a strange-sounding detail: Anthropic's IPO, still unpriced, is already being described as needing a valuation cut from the roughly $1.5 trillion level analysts had forecast. That's not a market reaction to a disappointing debut — it's happening before the deal even opens for trading, while Nvidia's leadership crisis and a broader AI-stock correction are unfolding around it. Understanding why a private valuation can move before a single public share trades requires understanding how IPO price discovery actually works, which is a mechanism every finance student eventually has to internalize before they ever touch a term sheet or a comps table.

An IPO's price isn't set by the company or even by the lead underwriters alone — it comes out of bookbuilding, a process where bankers canvass large institutional investors, show them a preliminary price range built off comparable-company multiples and a growth forecast, and ask how many shares they'd buy and at what price. Anchor investors — typically large asset managers or sovereign funds who commit early and signal confidence to the rest of the order book — carry outsized influence here: when enough of them push back on a number, underwriters either narrow the range downward or risk an undersubscribed, embarrassingly weak first trading day, which can impair the company's access to capital markets for years afterward.

The clearest historical analogue is WeWork's 2019 attempt to go public: the company entered the process targeting a roughly $47 billion valuation based on earlier private funding rounds, but as underwriters actually tested that number with institutional investors, the book came back supporting something closer to $10-15 billion, and the deal was pulled entirely rather than priced at the markdown. What's easy to miss is that the $47 billion figure was never wrong by some objective measure — it was simply a private-market price with no one required to actually transact at it, while public price discovery forces a real clearing price the moment real capital has to commit.

The same forcing mechanism is now hitting Anthropic, and it's informative precisely because it's happening in the same window as Nvidia's selloff and the Nasdaq's slide into correction: both are the public market applying a lower multiple to projected AI cash flows than it was willing to pay a few months ago. If Anthropic's roadshow confirms a materially lower clearing price — or the deal is postponed, as some reports suggest — that would be read as the IPO market's version of what equity investors are already doing to Nvidia: discounting the AI growth story for a higher cost of capital and more execution risk, which is the same repricing the Fed's hawkish rate path and the Dec. 8-9 meeting will keep testing across every AI-exposed asset.
